finding: The live range of $140-$825 is too low at both ends for replacing the whole fan assembly, and most clearly too low at the top. Built totals, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Nissan Sentra 1.8L about $226-$758 ($106 aftermarket to $534 Nissan list, 1.0-1.4 hr); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $236-$698 (1.0-1.5 hr); midsize 2016 Camry 2.5L about $222-$1,295 (0.9-2.1 hr), where the top is Toyota's five separate pieces at list (shroud, two blades and two motors, $959) because Toyota does not sell the fan as one assembly; luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $485-$1,211, which is BMW 328i parts ($389 aftermarket to $1,083 BMW list) plus 0.8 hr, a time stated for a comparable luxury vehicle (2014-2015 Mercedes-Benz S-Class), not for the BMW. The bottom: the cheapest total we can build is about $222-$236, and that pairs an online aftermarket price with a manufacturer warranty time or a seller's approximate time; $140 is below anything found for a full assembly. It is only reachable as a motor-only repair (a Four Seasons motor for the Camry is $56 and GM allows 0.6 hr to change one fan motor on a Tahoe), which is a different job from the one named here. The top: $825 covers an economy car or a truck fitted with dealer-list parts, but not the luxury class, where the BMW part alone lists at $1,083 (about $1,211 fitted), nor a Camry fitted with Toyota parts (about $1,180-$1,295). Every RepairPal figure is above the live ceiling ($839-$948 for a motor, $1,176-$1,306 for an assembly, $1,117-$1,243 for a 2016 Camry, $1,144-$1,173 for a 2015 328i xDrive); RepairPal assumes about $620-$900 in parts, close to dealer list, where a good aftermarket assembly for the same mainstream cars is $106-$240. A range near $225-$1,300 would fit the evidence better. How solid the labor times are: three of the eight range ends are now stated for the example vehicle or its own generation, and five are not, which is why confidence stays low. Economy: the example was changed from the 2015 Corolla to the 2017 Nissan Sentra because Toyota prints no time for the Corolla and Nissan does for the Sentra; the top (1.4 hr, fan shroud and motor assembly) is Nissan's own warranty time for the 2017 Sentra, and the low (1.0 hr) is a Kia warranty time for a 2012-2015 Rio (fan motor, including inspection and a software update), not a Sentra. Midsize: the top (2.1 hr) is Toyota's warranty time for a 2012 Camry 2.5L, the same generation and engine as the 2016 example, but it covers taking out and refitting both fans and replacing the A/C amplifier, so it overstates a plain assembly swap; the low (0.9 hr) is a Mazda warranty time for a 2019-2020 CX-5, not a Camry; FCA times of 1.3-1.4 hr for the Jeep Renegade, Fiat 500X and Ram ProMaster City sit in between. Truck: a parts seller's approximate 1-hour figure for the F-150 itself, repeated on three listings, and a GM recall time for a 2010-2014 Tahoe (1.5 hr, which also covers a wiring change); no Ford-stated time was found. Luxury rests on one figure: a Mercedes-Benz service campaign for the 2014-2015 S-Class allows 0.8 hr to replace the radiator fan. It is a manufacturer warranty time, but for a comparable luxury vehicle and not the BMW 328i, and the copy loaded is hosted on an owners forum; with only one figure the luxury hours are a single point, not a range. Switching the luxury example to the S-Class was considered and rejected because no aftermarket fan with confirmed fitment could be sourced for it. Four attempts found no stated time for the BMW itself: the BMW bulletin that replaces this very fan on the F30 gives the allowance as 'Refer to KSD2', and BMW's FRU figures were not converted because no loaded BMW document states the conversion. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, and a 2014 Jeep Wrangler bulletin allows only 0.3 hr, so easy-access fans can come in under these ranges. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis. Reviewer note (2026-11-20): the midsize high end was put back to 1.4 hr; Toyota's 2.1 hr for the 2012 Camry includes replacing the A/C amplifier and is kept as a cross-check only. Midsize built total about $222-$1,183.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis first, because a fan that will not run is frequently a relay, fuse, resistor, coolant temperature sensor, wiring fault or fan control module, not the fan itself (one GM bulletin allows 0.4 hr for a fan control module, and a Kia bulletin 0.5 hr for a fan resistor). On cars where the upper radiator hose or the radiator must come out to free the shroud, expect coolant, a top-up and bleeding of the cooling system. Also possible: a second fan or the air-conditioning condenser fan on dual-fan cars, new mounting clips or rubber mounts, wiring or connector repair where the plug has overheated, a refrigerant service if the condenser has to be moved, shop supplies and sales tax. A motor-only repair, where the motor is sold separately, costs much less than the assembly priced here.
